evidence.title: Implementation of an artificial intelligence-based system for mammography in the compulsory medical insurance program: results of a 3-year study
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.outcome: Calibration tests against predefined AUC/accuracy thresholds before CMI implementation
evidence.effect: First two calibration tests failed thresholds (CalT1 accuracy 0.77; CalT2 AUC 0.78, accuracy 0.74), triggering developer updates; third test passed (AUC 0.84, accuracy 0.81) before implementation.
evidence.quote: The first two calibration tests failed to meet the predefined performance thresholds (0.80).

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.outcome: Calibration testing against predefined AUC and accuracy-deviation thresholds before clinical integration
evidence.effect: Initial model fell below the AUC threshold (0.81). After developer updates, version 0.15.0 reached AUC 0.81 and no metric deviated >10%, enabling PACS integration.
evidence.quote: Initial calibration testing of the AI model yielded promising results; however, the AUC and relative accuracy deviation fell below the established thresholds ( Figure 5 a, Table 6 ).

evidence.title: SOS Dental Trauma-An Artificial Intelligence Chatbot via WhatsApp for Guiding Patients After Dental Trauma
evidence.venue: Dental traumatology : official publication of International Association for Dental Traumatology
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and completeness against a predefined 90% threshold in simulated cases, with revision and retest
evidence.effect: Permanent dentition met 100% accuracy and completeness initially. Primary dentition fell below the 90% threshold (luxation, displacement). After prompt revisions, all trauma types reached 100%.
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, it fell below the threshold in cases of primary dentition, particularly luxation and displacement, due to oversimplification of management options.

evidence.title: A simulation-based framework for sizing paired benchmarks in the evaluation of clinical artificial intelligence, applied to 168 expert-level dyslipidaemia items
evidence.outcome: Whether a priori bank sizing determined which paired-comparison conclusions were reachable
evidence.effect: Total architectural contrast resolved at 8.9 points with 97.7% realised power; orchestration-only contrast unresolved at 2.4 points, 13.3% power, needing ~1051 items. Of 13 contrasts, 5 resolved, 5 underpowered, 2 unresolvable, 1 hypothesis.
evidence.quote: Bank size, not the system under test, determined which conclusions were reachable.

commentary.bottom_line: Four studies, including two large mammography deployments in Russia, suggest that prespecified quantitative thresholds can hold back underperforming AI tools and prompt revision before go-live. No study compared prespecified evaluation with post hoc or unowned evaluation, so any effect on patient outcomes remains untested.

perspectives.view: The two largest tests are observational mammography studies in Russia (n=404,502 and 593,365) that applied predefined AUC and accuracy thresholds. A vignette study and a benchmark add indirect support. Certainty is low because no study had a post hoc comparison arm, both large studies share one country and modality, and outcomes measure the gate rather than patient harm.

In one mammography study the first two calibration tests failed (accuracy 0.77; AUC 0.78, accuracy 0.74), and implementation waited until a third test passed (AUC 0.84, accuracy 0.81). In another, an initial model below the AUC threshold was updated before PACS integration. In a dental simulation, primary dentition fell below a 90% threshold until prompt revisions. The gate may have stopped weaker versions before patient exposure.

A dyslipidaemia benchmark of 168 items found that a priori sizing decided which conclusions could be reached. Of 13 contrasts, 5 resolved and 5 were underpowered. One contrast had 13.3% power and would need about 1,051 items. An undersized test set may therefore leave a go-live decision without statistical support.

One Russian study required developer updates after two failed calibration tests before implementation, and the other required updates after an initial model fell below the AUC threshold before PACS integration. Organizations may need to plan for more than one evaluation cycle per tool. Neither study reported cost, staff hours, or delay to go-live, so the burden at health-system scale is unknown.

FDA draft lifecycle guidance asks sponsors to state null and alternative hypotheses, and CHAI frameworks require named owners for validation and monitoring. Both Russian studies report that clinical implementation or integration followed only after a model met predefined thresholds. This approach may inform procurement gates, although no study tested owner assignment directly.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized or compared prespecified acceptance thresholds against post hoc or absent criteria. No study tested whether assigning a named evaluation owner changes decisions. It is unknown whether passing a pre-go-live threshold predicts performance after deployment or reduces patient harm. No study measured the cost or time required to run repeated calibration cycles.
commentary.underserved_note: No test reported enrolling or analyzing Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two studies did not report a country or setting. A tool that meets an aggregate threshold may still underperform in these groups. Systems serving them would need to set subgroup-specific thresholds themselves, and no evidence yet shows whether doing so works.
